reference.source: Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: An X-linked hypomyelinating leukodystrophy caused by abnormalities of the PLP1 gene, most often a duplication rather than a point mutation
Affected boys typically present in infancy with nystagmus and hypotonia, later developing spasticity, ataxia, and cognitive impairment
Pendular nystagmus in early infancy is a characteristic early clue and may precede other signs
The severity spans a spectrum, from severe connatal disease to the milder allelic disorder spastic paraplegia type 2
This is a hypomyelinating disorder, so MRI shows a deficiency of myelin formation rather than active demyelination
PLP1 duplications generally produce the classic phenotype, while null mutations and some point mutations cause distinct and sometimes milder or peripheral-nerve-involving pictures
Diagnosis rests on the clinical picture, MRI evidence of hypomyelination, and PLP1 dosage and sequence analysis
Female carriers are usually asymptomatic but can occasionally show mild signs, and genetic counselling is important for at-risk families
reference.pathophysiology: Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease results from abnormalities of PLP1, which encodes proteolipid protein, a major myelin protein of the central nervous system produced by oligodendrocytes. Duplication, point mutation, or deletion of PLP1 disrupts oligodendrocyte function and myelin assembly, leading to failure of normal myelination (hypomyelination) rather than breakdown of previously formed myelin. Overexpression from duplication is toxic to oligodendrocytes, accounting for the common severe phenotype, while different mutation types produce distinct clinical severities.
additionalDifferentials: Cerebral palsy (for early hypotonia and later spasticity)
Mitochondrial and other early-onset white matter disorders
additionalInvestigations: PLP1 dosage analysis to detect duplication and sequencing for point mutations
Brain MRI demonstrating a hypomyelinating pattern
Assessment of nystagmus and visual pathways
Developmental and neurological evaluation over time
Genetic counselling and carrier testing for female relatives
redFlags: Severe connatal presentation with respiratory and feeding difficulty
Rapidly progressive spasticity limiting mobility and causing contractures
Failure to establish any developmental milestones
reference.prognosis: Outcome varies widely with phenotype; the connatal form carries a poor prognosis, the classic form progresses more slowly with survival into adulthood in some, and the allelic spastic paraplegia type 2 is milder. Care is supportive and directed at spasticity, feeding, and complications.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing early disease as cerebral palsy and not pursuing genetic testing
Relying on sequencing alone and missing a PLP1 duplication that requires dosage analysis
Confusing hypomyelination with active demyelination on imaging
Not distinguishing it from the clinically similar GJC2-related disorder
management: Manage spasticity with physiotherapy, antispasticity agents such as baclofen, botulinum toxin and orthoses to prevent contractures
Support feeding and nutrition, using gastrostomy where swallowing is unsafe, to counter failure to thrive
Provide respiratory care and treat recurrent aspiration and chest infections
Treat associated seizures and optimise posture, seating and mobility with occupational therapy
Coordinate multidisciplinary developmental, neurology and rehabilitation follow-up, as this hypomyelinating disorder has no disease-specific drug therapy
Offer genetic counselling for X-linked inheritance, with PLP1 carrier testing for female relatives and prenatal options
